text: 29 A number of studies also support the benefits of antiplatelet drugs for primary pre- vention of cardiovascular events in individuals at high risk. Aspirin may reduce the risk of first myocardial infarction in patients with stable chronic angina.30 The Thrombosis Prevention Trial31 in males at high risk of developing oc- clusive vascular disease and the Hypertension Optimal Treatment (HOT) trial32 in hypertensive patients have, more recently, confirmed that aspirin reduces the inci- dence of myocardial infarction in these at-risk groups, al- though both studies reported little or no effect on the over- all incidence of stroke. The Primary Prevention Project,33 a study in patients with at least one major risk factor, showed a reduction in cardiovascular mortality and in a composite of cardiovascular events including death, myo- cardial infarction, and stroke. Primary prevention in healthy individuals is more contro- versial, and studies have produced conflicting results. A study in healthy male physicians in the UK34 found no re- duction in the incidence of fatal and non-fatal myocardial infarction in those who had taken aspirin, while a similar study in the US35 showed a reduction in subjects 50 years of age or older; both showed a slight non-significant in- crease in the number of disabling strokes which, in the US study, were attributed to cerebral haemorrhage. In women, a large observational study in healthy US nurses36 indicat- ed that aspirin might reduce the risk of first myocardial in- farction, but a randomised trial37 found no effect on either myocardial infarction or death, although the incidence of stroke was reduced. Meta-analyses26,38,39 have generally concluded that for most healthy individuals, aspirin thera- py is inappropriate. Aspirin has been the most widely studied antiplatelet drug and appears to be effective over a range of doses (see p.24); however, some patients are resistant to its effects and remain at high risk for cardiovascular events.40 Other drugs may be used in those intolerant of aspirin, and com- bination therapy may also be considered. In the CAPRIE study,41 clopidogrel was shown to be at least as effective as aspirin in reducing cardiovascular events, including myo- cardial infarction and stroke, in individuals at high risk.
